usage: Used when discussing who should pay for environmental cleanups or climate change mitigation.
grammar_pattern: Subject + foot the bill + for + noun
common_mistakes: pay the bill for the environment
example_sentences: Governments should foot the bill for transitioning to renewable energy.
It is unfair for developing nations to foot the bill for climate damage caused by the West.
If companies pollute our rivers, they should be the ones to foot the bill for the cleanup.
We cannot expect the local community to foot the bill for a global environmental issue.
Taxpayers shouldn't have to foot the bill for industrial accidents.
collocations: foot the bill for climate change
foot the bill for environmental restoration
native_notes: A common idiom in professional contexts to describe accountability for financial consequences.

usage: Used when discussing the environmental impact of travel, diet, or lifestyle choices.
grammar_pattern: Subject + leave + a + adjective + carbon footprint
example_sentences: Every time we fly, we leave a significant carbon footprint.
We are trying to leave a smaller carbon footprint by cycling to work.
Modern agricultural practices often leave a massive carbon footprint on the planet.
It is hard not to leave a carbon footprint in today's globalised world.
Reducing your meat consumption is one way to lower the carbon footprint you leave behind.
native_notes: Very common in IELTS Speaking Part 3 and Writing Task 2 essays regarding sustainability.

usage: Used to describe the negative, gradual damage caused by pollution or human activity.
grammar_pattern: Subject + take a toll on + noun
example_sentences: Industrial waste is taking a heavy toll on our marine life.
Frequent wildfires are taking a toll on local forest ecosystems.
Urbanisation has taken a significant toll on biodiversity.
The heatwave is taking a toll on crop production this year.
Air pollution is clearly taking a toll on the health of city residents.
collocations: take a toll on the environment
native_notes: Often used with 'heavy' or 'significant' to emphasise the severity of the damage.

usage: Used in academic or social commentary to criticise the habits of excessive consumption and waste.
example_sentences: Our throwaway culture is directly responsible for the overflowing landfills.
To protect the planet, we must move away from our current throwaway culture.
Fast fashion is a classic example of modern throwaway culture.
The throwaway culture of the 21st century encourages us to replace gadgets constantly.
Policies should aim to penalise the throwaway culture prevalent in large corporations.
native_notes: Implies a negative value judgment on how people treat products as temporary rather than long-lasting.

usage: Used when describing species or ecosystems in critical danger of disappearing.
grammar_pattern: Subject + be + on the brink of + noun/V-ing
example_sentences: Many species are currently on the brink of extinction due to habitat loss.
The world's coral reefs are on the brink of total collapse.
We are on the brink of an environmental crisis if we do not act now.
Some island nations are on the brink of being submerged by rising sea levels.
The ecosystem was on the brink of recovery before the oil spill occurred.
native_notes: Dramatic and impactful phrasing, ideal for conclusions in essays.

usage: Used when discussing the impact of individuals, companies, or countries on climate change through emissions.
example_sentences: We are looking for ways to reduce our carbon footprint by cycling to work.
Airlines are under pressure to cut their massive carbon footprint.
Individual carbon footprints are much smaller than industrial ones.
Calculating your carbon footprint is a great way to start living more sustainably.
Government policies aim to lower the national carbon footprint by 2030.
native_notes: Very common in media and academic discussions; 'offset' is often used alongside it, meaning to pay for projects that remove carbon to make up for your own emissions.

usage: Used to describe adopting environmentally friendly practices in daily life or business.
common_mistakes: using it as a noun instead of a verb phrase
example_sentences: It's becoming much easier for households to go green these days.
Many companies are going green to attract eco-conscious customers.
We decided to go green by installing solar panels on our roof.
Going green doesn't have to be expensive or difficult.
The city council is encouraging local businesses to go green.
native_notes: This is a phrasal idiom. It is widely used in casual conversation and marketing but is slightly too informal for a high-level academic essay.
russian: переход к экологически чистому образу жизни

usage: Used when talking about taking action against the global warming crisis.
common_mistakes: saying 'solve climate change' (it's too complex to 'solve' easily)
example_sentences: International cooperation is essential to effectively tackle climate change.
Governments must do more to tackle climate change before it is too late.
Technological innovation is key if we want to tackle climate change.
Young activists are pressuring leaders to urgently tackle climate change.
Developing countries need financial support to tackle climate change successfully.
native_notes: 'Tackle' implies a difficult, multi-faceted struggle, which makes it perfect for climate discussions.

usage: Used in academic or formal contexts when discussing materials like fossil fuels, water, or minerals that will eventually run out.
example_sentences: Our planet has finite resources that we cannot continue to exploit.
We need to transition to renewable energy because fossil fuels are finite resources.
The rapid consumption of finite resources is a major threat to future generations.
Sustainability is about managing our finite resources more wisely.
Global economies are too dependent on finite resources.
native_notes: Very strong collocations with verbs like 'deplete' or 'exploit'. Highly recommended for IELTS Writing Task 2.

usage: Used to describe a methodology or strategy that minimizes environmental harm.
example_sentences: The architect took an eco-friendly approach when designing the new office block.
Adopting an eco-friendly approach to farming can preserve soil quality.
We should switch to an eco-friendly approach in our daily packaging.
This project requires an eco-friendly approach to waste management.
Many startups are built on an eco-friendly approach from day one.
native_notes: The hyphen is technically required as it functions as a compound adjective before the noun 'approach'.

expression: to be at a tipping point
usage: Used to describe a critical moment where a system is about to change irreversibly, often used in climate change discussions.
grammar_pattern: Subject + be + at a tipping point
common_mistakes: using it for minor daily problems
alternatives: past the point of no return
example_sentences: Many scientists argue that our planet is at a tipping point regarding global warming.
The delicate ecosystem of the rainforest is currently at a tipping point.
We are at a tipping point where immediate action is required to save the species.
Economic experts believe the energy sector is at a tipping point due to new regulations.
If we don't act now, we will surely pass the tipping point for biodiversity loss.
collocations: dangerously close to a tipping point
native_notes: It implies that once this point is passed, you cannot go back to the previous state.

usage: Refers to items like straws, bags, and cutlery that are used once and then thrown away.
common_mistakes: pluralising 'plastic' as 'plastics' in the wrong context
example_sentences: Many supermarkets are banning single-use plastics to reduce pollution.
The government introduced a tax on single-use plastics last year.
It is much better to carry a reusable bottle instead of using single-use plastics.
The oceans are currently overwhelmed by waste, much of which is single-use plastics.
We need to find sustainable alternatives to single-use plastics.
native_notes: In the UK, this is the exact phrase used in public debate and government policy.

usage: Used when something is causing damage, destruction, or exhaustion over a period of time.
grammar_pattern: Something + take a toll on + something/someone
example_sentences: Industrial waste is taking a toll on our local river system.
The prolonged heatwave is starting to take a toll on the region's crops.
Deforestation really takes a toll on wildlife habitats.
Constant noise pollution takes a toll on the health of people living in big cities.
Tourism in fragile environments can take a toll on local ecosystems if not managed well.
collocations: take a toll on the environment
take a toll on the economy
native_notes: This is a very common idiom used for everything from the environment to personal health.

usage: Used when stopping the use of something gradually rather than all at once.
example_sentences: The country plans to phase out coal power plants by 2040.
The company is phasing out petrol cars in favour of electric models.
We need to phase out toxic chemicals in our manufacturing processes.
The government is phasing out subsidies for fossil fuel industries.
Teachers are phasing out traditional textbooks for digital learning materials.
native_notes: This is preferred over 'stop' because it emphasises that the change happens over a long period.

usage: Used when describing products, habits, or policies that do not harm the environment.
common_mistakes: Using 'eco-friendly' as a verb (e.g., 'we eco-friendlied the office').
example_sentences: Many local businesses are now switching to eco-friendly packaging.
It’s surprisingly easy to lead an eco-friendly lifestyle in the city.
We need to invest in more eco-friendly transportation systems.
The new housing project is designed to be completely eco-friendly.
Are there any simple, eco-friendly swaps I can make in my daily routine?
native_notes: Very common in marketing and general conversation; it's a catch-all term for anything beneficial to nature.
russian: экологически чистый (не наносит вреда окружающей среде)

usage: Used in discussions about climate change and individual or corporate responsibility for emissions.
common_mistakes: Using 'carbon footprint' to mean pollution in general.
example_sentences: Traveling by train instead of flying helps reduce your carbon footprint significantly.
Governments are under pressure to help industries reduce their carbon footprint.
I've been trying to reduce my carbon footprint by eating less meat.
It is nearly impossible to reduce your carbon footprint to zero in a modern city.
The company claims that its new factory will drastically reduce its carbon footprint.
native_notes: Specifically refers to the amount of greenhouse gases produced by an entity; often used in debates about global warming.
russian: уменьшить выбросы углекислого газа (воздействие на окружающую среду).

usage: Used to describe modern cultures that prioritize disposable items over repairs or recycling.
grammar_pattern: We live in + a throwaway society
common_mistakes: Misunderstanding it as a place where people throw things away literally.
example_sentences: We need to move away from a throwaway society if we want to save resources.
Cheap electronics are a major reason why we have become a throwaway society.
Repairing items is becoming rare in our modern throwaway society.
The government is implementing policies to combat our throwaway society.
In a throwaway society, everything is designed to be replaced after a few uses.
collocations: the rise of a throwaway society
native_notes: This is a critical term used often in sociology or environmental science essays to describe the lack of durability in manufactured goods.

expression: to be on the brink of disaster
usage: Used when describing an ecosystem or the planet nearing a point of irreversible environmental damage.
grammar_pattern: Subject + be + on the brink of + noun
common_mistakes: Saying 'on the edge of disaster' (less common colocation).
example_sentences: Many scientists warn that our oceans are on the brink of disaster.
The local ecosystem is on the brink of disaster due to illegal logging.
We are currently on the brink of an environmental disaster if we don't act now.
Without strict regulations, the region is on the brink of ecological disaster.
The species is on the brink of disaster and needs immediate protection.
synonyms: at the point of no return
native_notes: Dramatic and impactful. Used to convey urgency; 'brink' implies a very narrow edge before a fall.

uzbek: tabiatga zarar yetkazmaydigan hayot tarziga o'tish
usage: Used to describe the act of adopting more environmentally friendly habits.
common_mistakes: using it in very formal academic writing
example_sentences: Our office decided to go green by banning single-use plastics.
It's becoming much easier to go green these days.
More families are choosing to go green to save money and the planet.
If everyone decided to go green, it would make a huge difference.
I'm really trying to go green by composting my food scraps.
native_notes: Informal and catchy; great for Speaking Part 1 or 2.
russian: переход к образу жизни, не наносящему вреда природе

usage: Used to describe severe negative consequences of an action on the environment or health.
grammar_pattern: Subject + take(s) a heavy toll on + Object
example_sentences: Industrial pollution has taken a heavy toll on the river's ecosystem.
Intensive farming practices take a heavy toll on soil quality.
Oil spills take a heavy toll on marine life for decades.
Climate change is already taking a heavy toll on coastal communities.
Deforestation takes a heavy toll on local biodiversity.
native_notes: Sounds much more natural and precise than just saying 'is bad for'.

usage: Used in academic or news contexts to describe species, habitats, or ecosystems under severe threat.
example_sentences: Many endangered species are currently in jeopardy due to rapid deforestation.
The future of the coral reefs is in jeopardy if sea temperatures continue to rise.
Local communities fear their way of life is in jeopardy from rising sea levels.
Without immediate action, the habitat of the arctic fox will be in jeopardy.
The biodiversity of the rainforest is in jeopardy because of illegal mining.
native_notes: More sophisticated than 'in danger'; implies a formal or serious context.

usage: Used when describing a major shift in a situation from negative to positive, often regarding environmental change.
example_sentences: International climate agreements might finally turn the tide on global warming.
Local recycling schemes are helping to turn the tide against plastic waste.
It will take global cooperation to turn the tide of biodiversity loss.
Can new renewable energy projects turn the tide on carbon emissions?
Scientists are optimistic that these reforestation efforts will turn the tide.
native_notes: An idiomatic expression that adds a sense of drama and significant change.

usage: Used to describe environmental issues that are becoming more widely recognised or serious over time.
example_sentences: Plastic pollution in our oceans is a growing concern for marine biologists.
The rapid decline in air quality has become a growing concern among local residents.
Deforestation remains a growing concern for global climate policy.
Water scarcity in the region is a growing concern that requires immediate action.
The impact of pesticides on local wildlife is a growing concern.
native_notes: Perfect for IELTS Writing Task 2 or Speaking Part 3 to introduce a problem before discussing a solution.

usage: Refers to the impact (usually negative) that human activities or businesses have on the planet, often used in 'carbon footprint'.
common_mistakes: not specifying what kind of footprint (e.g., carbon/ecological)
using it in a positive sense
example_sentences: We need to find ways to reduce the carbon footprint of our daily commute.
Every factory leaves a footprint on the surrounding landscape.
Tourists should aim to leave a smaller footprint when visiting protected areas.
The construction industry is trying to minimize its footprint on the environment.
Even small lifestyle changes can help reduce your ecological footprint.
native_notes: While 'leave a footprint' is metaphorical, 'carbon footprint' is the standard technical term in climate discussions.

uzbek: uglerod izini qoldirmoq (atmosferaga zararli gazlar chiqarmoq)
usage: Used when discussing the total amount of greenhouse gases generated by our actions.
example_sentences: Air travel leaves a significant carbon footprint compared to taking the train.
We should all look for ways to reduce our personal carbon footprint.
Large industrial factories often leave a massive carbon footprint.
The government is incentivizing businesses to minimize their carbon footprint.
Switching to electric vehicles is a great way to lower your carbon footprint.
native_notes: The phrase is metaphorical; 'carbon footprint' is now standard terminology in climate change discourse.
russian: оставлять углеродный след (выбрасывать вредные газы в атмосферу)

expression: to put a strain on nature
usage: Used to describe how human activity causes stress or damage to natural ecosystems.
grammar_pattern: Subject + put + a strain on + object
common_mistakes: using 'make a strain' instead of 'put a strain'
alternatives: place a burden on the environment
example_sentences: Rapid urbanisation is putting a huge strain on nature and local wildlife.
Overfishing continues to put a severe strain on our oceans.
Tourism in sensitive areas can put a strain on nature if not managed properly.
The demand for cheap meat puts a strain on nature due to land clearing.
We are putting a strain on nature that the planet cannot sustain.
native_notes: Very common in IELTS essays when discussing cause-and-effect relationships.

usage: Used when talking about the exhaustion or excessive consumption of earth's limited materials.
common_mistakes: using 'deplete' for money instead of physical resources
example_sentences: Industrial expansion is rapidly depleting natural resources like coal and oil.
We are depleting natural resources at a rate that the earth cannot replenish.
If we do not switch to renewables, we will continue to deplete natural resources.
The reckless way we deplete natural resources is stealing from future generations.
There is a growing concern about how we deplete natural resources globally.
native_notes: A very 'high-level' academic term that examiners love to see in Task 2 writing.

expression: foot the bill for environmental damage
uzbek: ekologik zararlar uchun to'lovni amalga oshirish
usage: Used in discussions about who should pay for cleanup or ecological repairs, often used in policy or academic debates.
grammar_pattern: Subject + foot the bill for + noun phrase
example_sentences: The government insists that major polluters must foot the bill for the environmental damage they cause.
It is unfair for local communities to foot the bill for cleaning up industrial waste.
Large corporations should be legally required to foot the bill for environmental damage.
When it comes to climate change, developing nations cannot afford to foot the bill for global warming.
The oil company has agreed to foot the bill for environmental damage after the spill.
native_notes: Idiomatic expression implying that the party responsible for the mess should be the one to pay, regardless of the difficulty.

usage: Used when institutions or countries are struggling to solve a difficult environmental problem.
example_sentences: Governments worldwide are currently grappling with how to reduce plastic waste.
The city is grappling with the severe consequences of recent flooding.
Scientists are grappling with the challenge of finding carbon-neutral energy sources.
Developing countries often grapple with balancing economic progress and environmental conservation.
We are grappling with the reality of climate change in our daily lives.
native_notes: More sophisticated than 'solve' or 'deal with'. It implies a long, arduous process of trying to figure something out.

usage: Used when describing something valuable that risks being lost or destroyed, such as the future of the planet.
example_sentences: The future of the Amazon rainforest is at stake.
With climate change, the lives of millions of people are at stake.
We must act now because our children's future is at stake.
There is a lot at stake if we continue to ignore pollution levels.
Biodiversity is at stake due to rapid deforestation.
native_notes: Suggests a higher sense of urgency and seriousness compared to just saying 'at risk'.

usage: Used to describe products, practices, or behaviours that do not harm the environment.
example_sentences: I always try to buy eco-friendly cleaning products for my house.
The new office building was designed to be as eco-friendly as possible.
Switching to an eco-friendly lifestyle is easier than most people think.
Many fashion brands are now promoting eco-friendly materials.
We should encourage businesses to adopt more eco-friendly production methods.
native_notes: Very common in everyday English. Use it as an adjective before a noun or as a predicate adjective after 'is'.

expression: to be on the brink of
usage: Used to describe a situation where a negative event (like extinction or environmental collapse) is about to happen.
grammar_pattern: be on the brink of + V-ing/noun
alternatives: to be on the verge of
to be on the edge of
example_sentences: The tiger is currently on the brink of extinction.
Our planet is on the brink of a climate catastrophe if we don't change our ways.
The lake is on the brink of ecological collapse due to chemical waste.
Scientists warn that the coral reefs are on the brink of total destruction.
We are on the brink of a new era of renewable energy technology.
native_notes: Dramatic and impactful. Reserve this for serious environmental warnings in IELTS essays.

uzbek: uglerod neytral bo'lish (atmosferaga chiqadigan zararli gazlar miqdori bilan ularning yutilishi tenglashishi)
usage: Used in business, political, and academic discussions about climate change targets.
alternatives: to have a zero carbon footprint
example_sentences: The company aims to be carbon neutral by the year 2030.
It is increasingly difficult for heavy industries to become truly carbon neutral.
Many cities are pledging to be carbon neutral to tackle air pollution.
Becoming carbon neutral requires a massive shift towards renewable energy.
Is it even possible for the aviation sector to be carbon neutral in our lifetime?
native_notes: Carbon neutral specifically refers to the balance of CO2, whereas 'net-zero' often implies a broader scope including all greenhouse gases.
russian: быть углеродно-нейтральным (количество вредных газов, выбрасываемых в атмосферу, равно их поглощению)

usage: Used when discussing waste management, recycling policies, and consumer habits.
example_sentences: Many countries are implementing bans on single-use plastic bags.
I try to avoid single-use plastic whenever I go shopping.
The accumulation of single-use plastic is destroying our marine life.
Is there a viable alternative to single-use plastic packaging?
We need to reduce our reliance on single-use plastic items.
native_notes: Very common in media and public policy debates regarding environmental protection.

usage: Used to describe the global collective effort to promote environmental consciousness.
example_sentences: The green movement has gained significant momentum in recent years.
More young people are joining the green movement to demand policy changes.
Critics of the green movement argue that it hurts economic growth.
The green movement is no longer just a niche interest; it's mainstream.
Advocates within the green movement are pushing for stricter regulations.
native_notes: Refers to the broader socio-political push for environmental sustainability.

usage: Used when describing the depletion of natural resources or supplies until nothing is left.
example_sentences: If we keep using up non-renewable resources, future generations will suffer.
We have used up all the clean water in this area due to over-farming.
It is alarming how quickly we are using up our planet's natural reserves.
Don't use up all the plastic bags; try to reuse them instead.
Factories often use up massive amounts of electricity during peak hours.
native_notes: More vivid than 'use'. It implies that the supply is finite and now gone.

usage: Describes products or practices that do not harm the planet.
example_sentences: We should switch to more environmentally friendly cleaning products.
The government is promoting environmentally friendly transport options like cycling.
It is becoming easier to find environmentally friendly packaging in supermarkets.
Designing environmentally friendly buildings is a priority for modern architects.
I try to make environmentally friendly choices whenever I shop.
native_notes: Often shortened to 'eco-friendly' in casual conversation.

expression: to be at the mercy of nature
usage: Used to express the helplessness of humans when facing extreme weather or natural disasters.
grammar_pattern: Subject + be + at the mercy of + noun
example_sentences: When a hurricane hits, islanders are entirely at the mercy of nature.
Farmers are often at the mercy of nature regarding the annual rainfall.
Modern technology helps, but we are still at the mercy of nature during storms.
Living in the mountains, you are constantly at the mercy of nature.
The earthquake reminded us that we are at the mercy of nature.
native_notes: Dramatic and often used in journalism or serious discussions about disaster management.

expression: to take a toll on the environment
usage: Used to describe how a specific activity or industry causes gradual damage or stress to nature.
grammar_pattern: Subject + take a toll on + noun
alternatives: have a negative impact on the environment
example_sentences: Overfishing is taking a heavy toll on the ocean's ecosystem.
Rapid industrialization has taken a toll on the local air quality.
Mining activities take a toll on the environment by stripping away topsoil.
If we don't act now, the pollution will continue to take a toll on our health.
The expansion of the city is taking a toll on the surrounding forests.
native_notes: This implies a cumulative, negative effect that happens over time.

usage: Often used in the context of 'carbon footprint' to measure the impact of human activities on the environment.
common_mistakes: using 'footprint' without specifying which type (e.g., carbon)
example_sentences: I am trying to reduce my carbon footprint by cycling to work.
Large corporations have a massive environmental footprint.
Eating locally-grown food is a simple way to lower your footprint.
Our daily consumption habits significantly increase our ecological footprint.
The government is implementing policies to track the industrial footprint of factories.
native_notes: Very common in media and academic discussions about sustainability.
russian: углеродный след / воздействие на окружающую среду

usage: Used when referring to resources, animal populations, or supplies that are steadily decreasing.
common_mistakes: using it for things that increase
example_sentences: Natural resources are starting to dwindle due to overconsumption.
The population of this endangered species has dwindled significantly over the last decade.
Water supplies in the region are dwindling because of the drought.
As the forest area dwindles, many animals lose their natural habitat.
Public interest in environmental issues seems to dwindle during economic crises.
native_notes: Conveys a sense of slow, continuous loss rather than a sudden drop.

usage: Used to describe the severe damage or destruction caused by natural disasters or pollution.
common_mistakes: mixing up the past tense 'wrought' with 'wreaked'
example_sentences: Plastic pollution continues to wreak havoc on marine ecosystems.
The storm wreaked havoc on the coastal villages last night.
Industrial waste often wreaks havoc on local water quality.
Uncontrolled deforestation can wreak havoc on regional biodiversity.
Climate change is beginning to wreak havoc on global food supplies.
native_notes: A very powerful collocation. 'Wreak' is almost exclusively used with the word 'havoc'.

usage: Refers to a lifestyle that attempts to reduce an individual's use of Earth's natural resources.
example_sentences: Adopting sustainable living practices can save you money in the long run.
More young people are embracing sustainable living to protect the planet.
Sustainable living is not just a trend; it is a necessity for the future.
She shares tips on sustainable living through her social media channels.
Transitioning to sustainable living requires small but consistent changes.
native_notes: Often linked to 'going green' but implies a more structural, long-term commitment to habits.

expression: to leave a small carbon footprint
usage: Used when discussing lifestyle choices that minimize one's environmental impact.
grammar_pattern: Subject + leave + a + adjective + carbon footprint
example_sentences: I try to leave a small carbon footprint by cycling to work every day.
Living in a smaller house is one way to leave a smaller carbon footprint.
Our company is committed to leaving a small carbon footprint by using renewable energy.
Eating locally grown food helps you leave a smaller carbon footprint.
It is challenging to leave a small carbon footprint in a modern industrial city.
native_notes: Very common in everyday conversation when talking about recycling, travel, or energy consumption.

usage: Used to describe people or brands that prioritize environmental safety in their choices.
example_sentences: Modern consumers are becoming increasingly eco-conscious about what they buy.
It is vital to be eco-conscious when planning large-scale infrastructure projects.
Many young people are very eco-conscious and support brands with green policies.
Being eco-conscious doesn't have to be expensive or time-consuming.
The hotel prides itself on being eco-conscious, using only solar power.
native_notes: Slightly more modern than 'environmentally friendly' and focuses on the mindset of the person.

usage: Used when describing a life pattern that avoids the depletion of natural resources to maintain ecological balance.
example_sentences: It is becoming easier to lead a sustainable lifestyle with current technology.
Our goal is to lead a sustainable lifestyle by reducing our plastic consumption.
Leading a sustainable lifestyle requires a change in daily habits.
Governments should provide incentives for citizens to lead a sustainable lifestyle.
I find that leading a sustainable lifestyle actually saves money in the long run.
collocations: difficult to lead a sustainable lifestyle
native_notes: The term 'sustainable' is a buzzword, often used in professional and social contexts regarding the future of the planet.

expression: to be on the brink of extinction
usage: Used when referring to endangered species or dying habitats that are very close to disappearing forever.
grammar_pattern: to be on the brink of + noun (extinction/collapse)
common_mistakes: saying 'on the edge of extinction' (brink is more common for this specific collocation)
using 'at the brink' instead of 'on the brink'
example_sentences: The Javan rhinoceros is currently on the brink of extinction due to poaching.
Without intervention, many coral reefs will be on the brink of extinction.
Conservationists are fighting to save species that are on the brink of extinction.
We must act now before these rare plants are on the brink of extinction.
Habitat loss has pushed several mammal species to the brink of extinction.
collocations: pushed to the brink of extinction
species on the brink of extinction
save from the brink of extinction
teetering on the brink of extinction
native_notes: Powerful, dramatic phrasing used in documentaries (like David Attenborough style) and academic essays.

usage: Used to describe who or what suffers the most severe impact from a negative event like climate change or pollution.
grammar_pattern: Subject + bear(s)/bore + the brunt of + noun/gerund
example_sentences: Developing nations often bear the brunt of climate change.
Coastal communities are currently bearing the brunt of rising sea levels.
Farmers in the region bore the brunt of last year's severe drought.
It is the poor who usually bear the brunt of environmental degradation.
If we don't act, our children will bear the brunt of our neglect.
collocations: bear the brunt of climate change
bear the brunt of the crisis
native_notes: Often used in news and academic essays to highlight unequal impacts of environmental issues.

usage: Used to describe environmental destruction or loss that is happening quickly and is concerning.
example_sentences: The rainforests are disappearing at an alarming rate.
Arctic ice is melting at an alarming rate due to global warming.
Wildlife species are becoming extinct at an alarming rate.
Plastic waste is accumulating in our oceans at an alarming rate.
Carbon emissions have increased at an alarming rate over the last decade.
native_notes: Used heavily in IELTS Speaking Part 3 and Writing Task 2 to show strong concern.

expression: to be in the same boat
uzbek: hammamiz bir qayiqdamiz (muammo barchamiz uchun umumiy)
usage: Used when discussing global environmental threats that affect everyone regardless of their location.
grammar_pattern: Subject + be + in the same boat
alternatives: We are all facing the same challenge
We are all in this together
example_sentences: When it comes to climate change, we are all in the same boat.
Developing nations and wealthy countries are in the same boat regarding rising sea levels.
It is no use pointing fingers; we are all in the same boat now.
Solving the biodiversity crisis is essential because we are all in the same boat.
We need global cooperation because, effectively, we are all in the same boat.
native_notes: Very common idiom; sounds natural in speaking parts 2 and 3.
russian: мы все в одной лодке (общая проблема для всех нас)

usage: Used to describe making a small but important personal contribution to a larger environmental effort.
example_sentences: I try to do my bit for the environment by recycling plastic.
Even if it is just a small gesture, everyone should do their bit.
We can all do our bit to reduce carbon emissions.
If every household does their bit, the impact will be huge.
Government policy is important, but citizens must also do their bit.
collocations: urge citizens to do their bit
do one's bit for the planet
do one's bit for the cause

expression: to be a drop in the ocean
usage: Used to describe an action that is too small to make a meaningful difference to a massive problem.
grammar_pattern: Subject + be + a drop in the ocean
common_mistakes: A little drop in the ocean
alternatives: insignificant compared to the scale of the problem
example_sentences: Cleaning up one beach is great, but it is just a drop in the ocean.
Our current recycling efforts are a drop in the ocean compared to industrial waste.
A few electric cars are a drop in the ocean when millions of petrol cars remain.
The small fine for the company was just a drop in the ocean of their profits.
We need systemic change; individual actions are often just a drop in the ocean.
collocations: be merely a drop in the ocean
seem like a drop in the ocean
just a drop in the ocean
hardly a drop in the ocean
felt like a drop in the ocean
native_notes: Great for expressing nuance in Speaking Part 3 or Writing Task 2.

usage: Used when talking about reconnecting with the environment or living a more natural, simplified life.
example_sentences: Many people move to the countryside to get back to nature.
Hiking in the mountains is a perfect way to get back to nature.
We built a vegetable garden because we wanted to get back to nature.
Living in a city makes it hard to get back to nature sometimes.
More tourists are seeking eco-lodges to get back to nature.
